articles.title: BRICKLAYERS.
articles.text:
THE BRICKLAYERS.

A crowded meeting of the members of the
Bricklayers' Society was holden Saturday night at
the Sussex Hall, Bouverie-street, Fleet-street, in
reference to the present state of affairs in the
building trade. Mr. Coulson occupied the chair,
and stated that on the 6th inst. the committee had
sent in a memorial to the Masters' Association for
the nine hours at 9d. per hour, with a code of
working rules for the regulation of overtime, &c.
The chairman and Mr. Batchelor were elected to
represent the trade on the united deputation to
wait upon the masters' committee next week. A
resolution was then adopted placing a levy of
is. 6d. per week on every member of the trade.
Another resolution was also adopted, strongly
condemnatory of the conduct of the masons.
The committee of masters having refused to
entertain the memorial aunt in by the bricklayers
on Monday, claiming a working day of nine hours,
at 9d. per hour, with a code of working rules for
the regulation of overtime and its payment, the
bricklayers' committee, acting upon a resolution
adopted at a general meeting of the trade on Satur-
day, struck against three London firms, who are
among the largest employers of bricklayers, and
Issued the following notice :
'
To Bricklayers in London.—
Fellow Workmen,
—The master builders of London having locked
out their bricklayers and other workmen, whether
members c.lr not of a trade society, showing clearly
they have no sympathy for your past services or
your wants other than using you as mere instru-
ments to gain them profit, we therefore appeal to
your manhood, and as bricklayers, to keep away
from the undermentioned builders' works until the
trade obtains a mutual settlement on the nine hour
day, 9d. per hour, and code of working rules.
Bricklayers, these firms lock out their men; keep
away from their works—Messrs. Rider and Son,
Union-street, Borough; Messrs. C. and W. Aldin,
South Kensington; Messrs. Jackson and Shaw,
Westminster. You are free to work at any other
firm in London except the above three. Unite and
succeed !—E. CouLsoN, Gen. See.
FRIDAY.—A meeting of the operative brick-
layers was held on Wednesday at Cambridge
Newman-street, Oxiord-street, Mr. John
Jeffery in the chair.
The Chairman explained that the object of the
meeting was to consider the position of the trade
in the present crisis.
Mr. Coulson, the secretary, stated that a memo-
rial had been sent in to the committee of masters,
requesting the nine hours at 9d. per hour, with a
code of working rules. To this memorial the
agreement with the masons was returned as an
answer; but the committee were not satisfied
with this reply, and made another application, that
six employers should be appointed to meet six
bricklayers, and see if an arrangement could not be
arrived at. The reply to that application was the
resolution passed by the masters' committee last
Monday. Three firms had therefore been struck,
and all tho men had come out. Ho regretted that
the masons and carpenters bad not accepted
arbitration, of which he was an advocate.
Mr. d. -Thompson then moved the following
resolution :
That we, the bricklayers of London, fully
endorse the action of our executive committee,
and pledge ourselves to give them every aid and
support in their endeavours to obtain for the
bricklayers the nine hours day, code of working
rules, and the Pd. per hour.
11G placed the code of rules before the pay,
considering it of more importance.
Mr. Paget seconded the resolution, which was
agreed to unanimously.
Mr. Batchelor then moved a resolution approving
the nation of the committee in striking the three
firms of Messrs. Rider and Co., Aldin and Co.,
and Jackson and Shaw, and pledging the meeting
to keep out of those firms and to use its influence
to induce all men in the trade to do likewise.
Mr. G. Gale seconded the resolution.

A diticugsion thou arose as to the expediency of
calling out all the men from these fii;ras which had
joined in the look-out, but it WU decided to be
undesirable to do so at present.

THE HOUSE PAINTERS.
The house-painters and decorators on Saturday
received a reply to their memorial from the Asso-
ciated iaster Painters, a body unconnected with
the Master Builders' Association. A few words of
explanation on the condition of the painters will
not be out of place hero. Several of the larger
master builders, such as Cubitt and Co., Trollope
and Co., and Smith and Taylor keep a staff of
house-painters in their regular employ, but the
great majority of the trade give their painting and
decorating work to be executed by firms who con-
fine their business to that single branch. There
aro about twenty of These large painting and deco-
luting firms in the metropolis, such as Morant and
Co., Craco and Co., Gillow and Co., Jackson and
Graham, S:e. It was ta these firms that the
painters sent in their memorial, as the hours
Nyotkerl and the wages paid by them would rega-

late those of painters generally. The memorial
claimed nine hours per day, or 51 hours per week,
at 81d. per hour, with a code of working rules.
The associated masters, in reply to this memorial,
conceded the 51 hours, but at Bd. per hour only.
This proposal will be laid before a general meeting
of the men for consideration. The standard
rate of wages for house- painters is always a half-
penny per hour under the men in the other
branches of the trade, though the men emyloyed
in the more artistic branches—such as graining,
pencilling, Bco —generally make their own terms,
and often receive is. and more per hour.
The painters paid their men on strike 9s. per
man,

articles.title: PLASTERERS.
articles.text:
THE PLASTERERS.

The Plasterers' Committee have issued a notice
to the trade, stating that in consequence of the
unsettled state of affairs in the building trade,
and the number of men still on the funds, the
levy of 3s. per week will be continued until
further notice. They have sent in a memorial
to the masters of the same nature as the brick-
layers, and have elected their representatives on
the united deputation.
The plasterers' dividend paid on Monday was

Gs. per man.
On Wednesday night a general meeting of
operative plasterers was held in the Berner's
Hall, Agricultural Hall, Islington. Mr. Sams-
bury in the chair.
The Chairman said the recent lock-out, conse-
quent upon the action taken by the carpenters,
had come upon the plasterers by surprise, and the
committee had since been engaged in organizing
the trade and providing support for the men who
were locked out. The men were now at work
again pending the course that might be taken by
the committee. The committee had sent two of
its members to represent the trade on the conference
of the building trades, in furtherance of the
movement for the nine hours at 9d. per hour, with
a code of working rules, and had sent in a memo-
rial to the employers requesting those terms.
Mr. ,Westohy thought the meeting should
pledge itself to support the committee in its
efforts to obtain the nine hours and the 9d.
Mr. Pugh approved the terms obtained by the
masons, but objected most strongly to the manner
in which they had obtained them. Ho thought
they might accept the 80. per hour now, and
agitate for the other id. on the first oppor-
tunity.
Mr. Lambert was in favour of the committee
agitating for the nine hours and the ninepence,
but was opposed to calling out the men at work
before they had the funds to support them.
Mr. Bishop was in favour of accepting the
masons' terms for the present.

A long discussion ensued, !during which it ap-
peared that the meeting was generally in favour
of the nine hours and the ninepence, but opposed
to calling the men out at present.
Mr. Hutchinson then moved:—

That power be given to the committee to use its
best efforts to obtain the nine hours, but in no
way to interfere with the men now at work.
A member in the body of the hall seconded the
resolution, which, after some further discussion,
was agreed to.

A. levy of Gd. per day to support the men now
out was then agreed to, and the proceedings closed
with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

We are requested by Mr. Westoby to announce
that the Plasterers, Clifton-villa, Brighton, have
subscribed .£1 19s. 10d.

articles.title: LABOURERS.
articles.text:
THE LABOURERS.

On Saturday morning the labourers who remain
upon strike sent in a memorial-to the masters'
committee claiming the nine hours, with an
uniform rate of wages at 6d. per hour (the present
rate varying from 4id. to old. per hour), and
extra payment for overtime.
A crowded meeting of the building labourers
was held on Wednesday night in the hall of the
Working Men's Club, Broadwall, Stamford-
street, when the reply of the Masters' Committee
to the memorial for an advance of wages to Gd.
per hour was read. The present rate of wages
varies from 4•lrd. to 6d. per hour. The masters
offered an advance of one farthing par hour. It
was contended that if the working hours were
reduced to nine per day, this advance of one
farthing would really be a loss in wages, on an
average, of 6s. per week. A resolution was
unanimonsly adopted adhering to the claim of 6d.
per hour. A resolution was also adopted for
calling an aggregate open-air meeting of building
labourers. A resolution for calling out the
labourers in seine of the large firms stood over for
further consideration,

'rho lubourors who have refused the offer from
the employers of an advane of ong farthing per
hour, and nailero to their demand of Ga. per hoar,

are arranging for a meeting in Trafalgar -square,
to consider the propriety of a general strike.
The usual dividend of 2s. ad. per man was paid
yesterday.

articles.title: JOINT COMMITTEE.
articles.text:
THE JOINT COMMITTEE.

The conference of the building trades met on
Monday afternoon at the Brown Bear, when the
delegates present were—Messrs. Sinclair and
Westoby, plasterers; Baker and Leverett, metal
workers; Shipton and Watkin, painters; and
Kenny, labourers. Mr. Shipton occupied the
*hair. The present position of the dispute was
carefully reviewed, and after some discussion
the following resolutions were unanimously
adopted :-
1. That this meeting of trades delegates hereby
resolves itself into an Amalgamated Building
Trades Committee, with Mr. Sinclair as chairman,
Mr. Shipton as secretary, and Mr. Westoby as
treasurer.
2. That the secretary, Mr. Shipton, be instructed
to communicate with Mr. S. Bird, the secretary of
the Masters' Association, requesting that an early
day may be arranged to receive a joint deputation
from this committee to confer with the Masters'
Committee, on the terms of our memorials, with
the view to a settlement of the existing dispute in
the building trade.
3. That the secretary be instructed to draw up
a circular announcing the formation of the com-
mittee, and appealing for pecuniary support to the
entire country.
4. That no branch of the building trade repre-,
sented on this committee shall enter into any
negotiations with the master builders, or the
Master Builders' Association, relative to the pre-
sent dispute, other than through the duly-
appointed officers of the committee.
The conference broke up at 6 o'clock, imme-
diately after which Mr. Shipton posted the letter
to Mr. Bird, the Masters' secretary, requesting an
interview for the joint deputation :
Stu,—l have the honour to inform you that to-day
a Central Amalgamated Committee has been formed
of delegates from the following branches of the
building trade—bricklayers, carpenters and joiners,
painters, plasterers, labourers, and motel workers.
I am requested by the committee to express our
desire that you will be good enough to arrange
some convenient time on an early da) for an
interview between the Master Builders' Association
and a joint deputation from the trades composing
this committee, for the purpose of considering the
terms of our memorial and working rules, with
the view to the settlement of the present dispute.
The answer of Mr. Bird, received on Tuesday,
was as follows :

In reply to your note of yesterday, I have to
draw your attention to the resolution of our com-
mittee of master builders passed yesterday. You
request an interview with a view of considering
the terms of your memorials, which memorials
have been fully considered already at lengthened
interviews with deputations from the carpenters
and joiners, and also the masons. if you think it
desirable to put in writing any distinct points
you think have not been considered already, I will
lose no time in laying such an application before
my committee, whose next mooting will be on
Monday next. I hog to remind you that no lock-
out exists in London at the present time."

The resolution referred to by Mr. Bird is the
first of those published under the proceedings of
the masters.

A meeting of the Amalgamated Building
Trades' Committee was held yesterday afternoon
at the Brown Boar, Bloomsbury. The delegates
present were—Messrs. Sinclair and Barry, car-
penters; Shipton and Watkin, painters; Leveret
and Vivian, metal workers; Westoby and Sains-
bury, plasterers; Coulson and Batchelor, back-
layers; and Kenny and Halloran, labourers.
Mr. Sinclair occupied the chair. Mr. Shipton,
the secretary, reported tho receipt of a letter from
Mr. Bird, the masters' secretary, declining to

receive a joint deputation from the committee to
discuss the memorials, as requested. The letter
elicited no discussion, and was ordered to lie upon
the table.
Several letters were read from trades and trades

councils in the provinces, pledging their pecuniary

support. It was resolved that a general appeal to
the country should be issued by the committee,
the subscriptions resulting from which should be
divided, pro rata, among the trades engaged in
the struggle.
The subject of holding an aggregate meeting of
the London trades Was thou discussed; and it was
unanimously resollied
That a mass meeting of the London trades he
held in Hyde Park • on Saturday, the 27th inst.,
.at ö o'clock in the evening. That each trade
attending be requested to bring its trade banners
and baud."

The remainder of the sitting was occupied with
routine business.

articles.title: COAL MINERS.
articles.text:
THE COAL MINERS.

SOUTH YORKSHIRE MINERS.

On Monday the annual procession, meeting,
and gala of the members of the South Yorkshire
Miners' Association took place at Barnsley. There
were many causes for the unusual success attend-
ing the gathering. The weather was a delightful
change to that of the past week; the association
never occupied abetter position as regards finances;
trade continues brisk, the miners are sharing in
its briskness, and the relations between employers
and employed was the general subject of con-
gratulation at the meeting. Fully 9,000 colliers
and boys took part in the procession, and to state
that in addition half of that number of women
and other friends of the colliers in the district
were assembled in Barnsley to witness the gather-
ing, is by no means an excessive estimate of the
people present. The instructions issued by Mr.
Normansell and Mr. Casey, the joint secretaries of
the association, for the guidance of the members,
were carried out with good order and regularity.
The members of lodges in the district met at their
lodge-houses as early as eight o'clock, and walked
in procession to Barnsley. Others from a distance
travelled by the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lin-
colnshire, the Midland, and the Lancashire and
Yorkshire railways, and were billeted, under
previous arrangement, at public-houses appointed
for each; and a given time was fixed for the re-
assembling of the lodges, and their march in pro-
cession to the Church-field, preparatory to a
general procession through the town to Queen's
Ground, where the annual meeting was held in
the afternoon. The lodges, accompanied by their
bands, met in the Church-field at midday, and,
when assembled with their banners and flags, made
quite an imposing show. Between seventy and
eighty collieries, the miners of which are members
of the association, sent representatives. The
following is a list of the lodges present, and the
bands heading each in the procession :

Wharnc Silkstono Band, Wharncliffe Silk.
stone Lodge, Rawmarsh Band, Rawmarsh and
Kilnburet Lodges ; Swinton Band, Swinton,
Worsbro' Park, and High Royd Lodges; Womb-
well Band, Wombwell Main Lodge ; Barnsley
Corporation Band, Blacker Main and Darley
Main Lodges; High Green Band and Thorneliffe,
No. 1 Lodge; Ardsley Band, Ardsley Oaks and
New Oaks Lodges; Dodworth Band, Strafford
Main and Rockley Lodges; Brightside Band,
Thryberg Hall Lodge; Barnsley Rifle Band, and
Edmunds Main Lodge; Hoyland Band, Hoyland
and Elsecar, Victoria, and Smithy Bridge Lodges;
Mapploweil Band, East Gawber and North
Gawber Lodges, Barnsley Temperance Band,
Mount Osborne and Agnes Main Lodges; Don-
caster Ride Band and Darfield Main Lodge; Crane
Moor Band, Stainbro', Levitt Hagg, and High
Stile Lodges; Eollesfield Old Band and Aldwarke
Main Lodge, Killamarsh Band, Silkstone Pall,
Woodthorpe and Killatnarsh Lodges ; Silkstone
Band, Old Silkstone No. 1, No. 2, and Pinder
Oaks Lodges; Ecclesheld Now Band, Lundhill
Lodge, Dewsbury Band; Willow Band, Monkhrettou
and West Ardsley Lodges; High= Band, Higham
and Silkstone Main Lodges, Prince of Wales Band,
and Low Ground Lodge; Grimestherpo Band and
Brightside Lodge; Rotherham Borough Band,
Carr House and Rosa Lodges, Chesterfield `United
Band, Tinsley Park New Whittington and
Unstono Lodges; ShOffield Druids' Band, Manor,
Havercroft, and Round Wood Lodges; Scholes
Band, Grange and Church-lane Lodges, Thorn-
clan Victoria Band, and Thorncliffe No. 2 Lodge;
Intake Band and Hollings End Lodge; Doncaster
Brass Band and Denaby Main Ledge; Waal Band,
Manvers Main Lodge, Woodhouse Band, Hands-
worth, Woodhouse, and S wallow Nest Lodges;
Greasbro' Band, Stabbin No. 1 and No. 2 Lodges;
Kirkburton Band, Woolley and Darton Lodges,
Wentworth Band, and Elsecar Lodge.

The procession left the Church-field at one o'clock,
and marched through the principal thoroughfares
to the Queen's Grounds. The men marched four
abreast, and fully three-quarters of an hour passed
before the rear of the procession left the place of
meeting. Many of the banners beading the lodges
were well designed and coloured. The eight
hours movement, the establishment of courts of
conciliation and arbitration, and the desirableness
of due attention being paid to the weighing of the
coal at bank, seemed to be the favomite subjects
commending themselves to the designers of the
banners. In some instances, however, not Ably
the banners of the Edmunds' Main, the Oaks, and
New Oaks Lodges, remembrances of past disasters
wore awakened by records of members lost on
each occasion. The remainder of the banners
were of the usual description borne in processions
on such occasions; suggesting unity, assistance
to sick members, and protection to the widows and
orphans. The streets were crowded during the
time the procession passed through the town.
The wives of the miners were not allowed to take
Part in the procession, but joined the processionists
at the meeting in Queen's Grounds. The num-
ber of persons present was considered to exhibit a
substantial increase upon the attendance of last

yeur.
At the meeting Mr. John 'ryas (Nlayor of

Barnsley) occupied the chair, and in opening the
meeting, expressed the pleasure he felt in presiding
on such an occasion as the chief magistrate of a
town so much indebted to the mining interest for
its vast increase in population, wealth, and pro-
sperity. (Cheers.)
Mr. John Normansell, one of the secretaries of
the association, then made a statement respecting
the amount of funds expended during the past ten
months, and the present position of the association.
He said that the weekly allowances to members
injured while following their employment had
been £1,661 10s. ; tho weekly allowances to
members sick from natural causes, £1,697 12s.
10d. ; funeral allowances, £743; grants to chari-
table purposes-old and injured members, &c.,
£410; weekly allowances to widows and orphans,
£1,224 14s. ; or a total for charitable purposes of
£5,637 58. 10d. Check-weighmente wages, £3,293;
and weigh books and stationery, £215 12s. 6d. ;
total £3,508 12s. sd. To members out of work
in consequence of disputes, the small amount of
£92 3s. 2d. :-(cheers)-granted to assist other
trades, £lBO 10s. ; total £272 13s. 2d. Cost of
arbitration in settling disputes, £lBO 7s. 9d.; paid
to Miners' National Association, £5O; expenses
of last demonstration, £680; law eases and sundry
expenses, £287 45. sd. ; general expenses, includ.
log officers' salaries, district committees' wages
and railway fares, printing and postage, carriage
of parcels, telegrams, deputations, and all other
general expenses, £384 16s. I Id. ; delegates' wages
and railway fares to and from council meetings,
£403 12s. 7d.; local committees' allowances at 63
lodges, £3lO 13s. lid.; salaries of local secretaries
and treasurers, £364 178. 3d.; rent of meeting rooms,
£56 Is. 4d.; £1,520 2s. The money saved during the
last ten months had been £6,000. (Cheers.)
Total, £18,136 ss. 7d. (Cheers.) He adied that
he was gratified in being able to sly that the past
year had been the most prosperous one ever
known to the working miners in the pits of South
Yorkshire. (Cheers.) Since their last meeting
they had received 20 per cent. as a direct advance
in wages, and there was no need to tell many of
his friends ho saw before him that they were not
satisfied with that amount, but wanted more.
(Laughter and cheers.) His advice' to them was,
that if more must come it should come without
creating any serious contention between employers
and employed. (Hear, hear.) Lot it come in the
future as in the past; they had not lost a single
day's work to gain the present 20 per cent., and
such a fact made the gain additionally satisfactory.
(Cheers.) He congratulated them upon the balance
sheet of the association, and particnlarly upon the
comparatively small item of £92 3s. 2d. paid to
members out of work in consequence ot strikes.
(Cheers.) They had a thousand members more
than last year, and were rapidly spreading the
operations of the associatiou Ira ll.a.byshire.
Mr. S. Hall, Holmes colliery, morel; Mr. C.
Moore, Rawmarsh, seconded; and Mr. W. Brown,
North Staffordshire, supported the adoption of the
report and a resolution urging the extension of
the operations of the association by every legiti-
mate means.

Mr. Brown, in speaking to the resolution, said
that the amount paid to members out of work in
consequence of disputes averaged 2id per head
among the whole of the members.
The resolution was adopted.
Mr. I. Ohitield, Pitsmoor, moved, and Mr. W.
Longley, Higham, seconded, the following reso-
lution :

That this meeting having heard the small
amount of money which has been expended in

SATURDAY, JULY 20, 1872.

THE DISPUTE IN THE BUILDING

TRADES.

UNFORTUNATELY, no progress has been
made towards the settlement of this most
unhappy difference between the employers and
the men of the building trades. Last week
but one we tendered our advice very frankly
and plainly. We said then, and we repeat
now, that the prolongation of this strike can do
nothing but harm, may in fact, be accompanied
by most deplorable loss to the one side, and
suffering on the other. The condition of
trade must make
.this dispute a serious incon-
venience to a vast number of people; and,
therefore, common-sense, as well asthe require-
ments of business and the comfort of poor
men's homes, demand that it should be settled
as soon as possible.
It would not become us to suggest any
method of settlement other than that we have
already thrown out. We need not repeat it ;
but we urge that something like it, if the
thing itself be not inadmissible, should
be attempted. The employers ought to
listen if the men make any reasonable
proposal to open the question—and if they
do not the blame will rest with them. If,
however, the men obstinately refuse to accept
arbitration in any form, if they will fight the
battle out to the end, without seeking
reasonably to bring it to a close, those who
are in the management of affairs run the risk,
if they lose the fight, of forfeiting for ever
the confidence of those they are now loading.

trtapr 20, 1872.'

RISE IN COALS.

TAXING the specimen we have already had
of the tendency in coals to rise in price, it
would not, we think, be amiss if housekeepers
in London and elsewhere were to take thought
for the coming winter. House coals have already
gone up from Os. to 10s. a ton in iLondon,
whilst those who profess acquaintance with the
subject give us the disquieting assurance that
should next winter turn out to be of more than
ordinary severity, coals will be sure to reach so
high a price as to be out of the reach of the
poorest portion of our population. Three
guineas per ton, it is said, will be a common
price, and with this extraordinary advance on
an article SQ necessary for the winter comfort
of the masses of our people, added to the
advances taking place in relation to every
other article of household consumption, people
are justified, notwithstanding the prosperous
condition of the country generally, in the
apprehensions they entertain as to an ap-
proaching period of great suffering amongst
the most needy portion of our population.

Already this rise in the price of coals is
attributed to the great advanDe which has
taken place in the wages of our colliers.
"Here," cry the enemies of trades unionism,
"may be seen in part that which must operate
over the whole field of production if trades
unions continue to force up unduly the rate of
wages amongst working men." On the face of
it this looks plausible -enough, and when we
take into account the constant cry of alarm
kept up as to combinations and strikes, it is
no wonder that a stupid craze of this kind
should take possession of people's minds.
Were coal an article in which there was any
kind of foreign competition there would be a
universal shriek as to the trade leaving the
country, in consequence of the aotion of trades
unionism. As it is, that frantic and foolish cry
cannot be raised, and we may, therefore,
more calmly look into the circumstances
of the case with the view of ascertaining
correctly how this wonderful enhancement
of price in coal has been brought about.
Our coal mines, as a. rule, are held for
terms of years, and, therefore, exorbitant
conditions imposed by proprietors cannot
have led to increase of price. The activity of
demand caused to a large extent by the brisk-
ness of the iron trade will have stimulated.
, demand, and thereby almost necessarily some-
what forced up prices. But in no way can
I this extraordinary advance, which has taken
I place, be attributed to the unreasonable de-
mands of the workmen.

A collier's wages per day will, perhaps,
amount to an average of five shillings; but
that there may be no chance of dispute, suppose
we put them down at six shillings. Twenty
per cent, of an advance on this would
amount to, say, Is, 3d. per day, making the
wages in full 7s. 3d, This is a very much
exaggerated view of the case, as we need
hardly say that colliers wages at the present
moment do not amount to anything like this,
which would give £2 33, 6d. as a week's
earnings. We believe that in the ordinary
mines a collier can put out eight tons of coal
a day, or in the week 48 tons. In a published
report of a Miners' Congress held in 1803 at
Leeds, we find that the amount of coal sent out
of the " Wombwell Main Colliery" iii a week
by six steady working colliers, was 6751 tubs
(of 10i owt. each),whieh, divided by six, would
give to each man 109 tubs, or 541 tons, or at
the rate of ten pence per ton as the gross sum
paid in collier's wages for each ton of coal
sent from the pit-bottom to the bank, If we
start, therefore, from the high level of wages
we have taken as the basis of our calculation,
and presume an advance of ten per cent.,
it will be seen that it would only add one
penny to the cost of the coals per ton, and yet
it is in an additional trifle like this that an
excuse has been found for the extra shillings
charged to the public by colliery owners and
coal dealers.

Here, therefore, we have an advance not
justified by cost of material, if ouch a word
may be used in reference to coal, not justified
by any circumstance whatever but increased
demand, and yet the coalowner and the coal
merchant try to put the blame of the enormous
tax they are levying on the public on the poor
collier's back, instead of frankly admitting
that the plunder, with scarcely twy dimunition

through increased wages, is flowing directly
into their own pockets. We are quite willing
to admit that house coals are but a portion of
the gross out-put, still, whatever the relative
value of the various kinds of "hard" "soft,"
and "slack," the cost of wages over the whole
cost of the article remains the same, and it
forms no real excuse, not even the shadow of
an excuse, for the exorbitant extortion of
wale wners and coal merchants.

There is one effectual way of checking this
system of public plunder now showing itself
in so dangerous a manner. Why not at once
organize great co-operative coal companies ?
Why not oo•operative collieries? Half a dozen
of these would put a stop for ever to such
scandalous impositions. In London three
millions of people depend for their winter
comfort on a full and cheap supply of coal,
and yet we allow colliery owners and coal mer-
chants, who have nothing but their own
interests to consider, to torture the poor by
putting fuel, by highness of price, beyond
their reach, and to prey upon the well-to-do
by making them pay double its value for the
coals needed for consumption in their house-.
holds, to say nothing of the serious damage
done to the manufacturing and commercial
interests of the country by overcharge on so
necessary and important an article as coal.
This is a serious matter, and the country
ought to look to it. It is the merest sham to
pretend that colliers' wages in any way cause
this state of things. Monopolists are taking
advantage of briskness of demand, and the
best check will be found in the opening of a
few co-operative collieries, which, by their
equitable working, would effectually protect
the general public from such shameless fraud.

articles.title: BUILDERS' LABOURERS AND
articles.text:
THE BUILDERS' LABOURERS AND

THE STRIKE.

A CROWDED meeting of labourers connected
with the building trades was held last week
in the large room of the Working Men's Club,
Broadwall, for the purpose of promoting
union amongst the men, and with the view of
giving them more power than they at present
possess over their own position whenever
disturbances arise between employers and
employed in the branches of industry with
which they are-conneeted.
It would bo difficult to imagine anything
more deplorable than the condition of these
men at the present moment, and it is
the more to be regretted inasmuch as what
they are now suffering they are always subject
to suffer when a strike or lock-out takes
place, although they themselves have no-
thing to do with
.the promotion of such
quarrels, and possess no power whatever that
could be profitably used for their prevention
or settlement. In arguing any point in dispute
between skilled artizans and their employers,
it is usually found that sometimes one party is
in fault and sometimes the other. We make
this admission very frankly, for, though
representing the cause of labour, we do
not feel in anyway bound to justify work-
ing men's faults or encourage their un-
reasonableness. But, however blame may be
apportioned between those who enter directly
into those conflicts in support of their con-
flicting interests, it is plain that no part of
that blame can be placed at the door of the
labourers. They are truly between hammer
and anvil; whichever party strikes or resists,
they feel the ooneussion and, suffer the pain.
However they may objoot, they must submit
to idleness and hunger whenever a strike or
look-out occurs, and they can only regain
employment and food when by the will or
through the necessities of other it terminates.
They naturally feel that this position is as
bad as it can be, and they want to alter it.
They feel, however, that there are many
difficulties in their way. They cannot help
being conscious that they are for the most
part entirely uninstructed, and possess, as a
matter of course, the usual drawbacks of such
a condition. Then their means are limited,
and worst of all, as an impediment to initia-
tion, their habits of thought and life render
them unfitted for mutual trust and joint
action. Still, at a time like the present, when
the spirit of union seems to be finding its way
in all directions, and when its power for good.
has been so dearly manifested, there is no

sufficient roason why these labouring men
ihoald not seek energetically to do on their

own behalf what more favourably situated
bodies of men find so much profit in.
It is undeniable that present circumstances

are greatly in their favour. In the past the
country always possessed a large surplus of
unskilled, and it may be added, of unem-
ployed labour. A large portion of this poured
in from Ireland, but this source has been
almost entirely dried up by the great outflow
to America, which has been going on for so
many years. Our English agricultural
labourers do not take kindly to labouring
work in the big towns, and they, like their
brethren of Ireland, rather look to emigra-
tion and to other employments, in our
largo towns, rather than to the hod and
the pick for their support. Our town labour-
ers, in fact, are less pressed on now than at
any former period. They may, in fact, be
said to have little to contend with beyond the
obstacles placed in their way by improvidence
and distrust.

Under these circumstances they are bound
to make a sensible manly effort for the
purpose of improving their position. Others,
it is true, may help them when they set about
the work, but if they mean to be successful
they must start it and continue it vigorously
themselves. They ought to got into their
minds as simply, but as firmly as possible,
the idea of union, not in any complicated way
as to aims, objects, and plans; an organization
and subscription first, and necessary drill to
enable them to work together; good leaders
whom they must trust and not suspect;
moderate rather than extreme counsels; a
disposition to expect little rather than mach
from their union at first. Let them suppose
that, instead of trying to begin this good work
now, they had started five years ago, and that
they had now an efficient organization and a
tolerably full exchequer. As a matter of
course, they would have to accept their
situation as they now accept it from the
employers and skilled operatives. But when
these parties had terminated their quarrel
and had agreed to commence operations
again, they would be in a position to
say to them—" Gentlemen, you began this
quarrel without reference to us; wa have lost
and suffered much by it, and now, before we
go in, you must pay us higher wages, as com-
pensation for what we have innocently suf-
fered through your stupidity in not being able
to settle your differences without strikes and
lock-outs." A. lesson of this sort, given as the
labourers could give it if in union, would
cause both parties to pause before they entered
on any new conflict, and put to themselves a
question or two as to how the labourers
might not; and in this way the labourers
would gradually be brought to have a voice,
and a very important one, in such disputes as
Might arise between employers and employed
in the building trades.
We hope the labourers will consider these
things, and set to work without loss of time
to form such a union or unions amongst them-
selves as will render a recurrene e of the dis-
advantages and privations they now suffer
difficult in the future.

articles.title: TaE BUILDERS' TRADES
articles.text:
TaE BUILDERS' TRADES

CIRCULAR AND THE BEE-HIVE.
MR. MAUL; in the Builders' Trades circular
of last Saturday, calls our remonstrance against
the general look-out, which he recommended
to the employers, "Balderdash." Wo shall
not quarrel with this gentleman about a matter
of literary style. Even if his charge be true
and his epithet correct we prefer being wrong
in taste to being wanting in humane Consider-
ation for the suffering even of those whom we
may hold accountable for bringing their mis-
fortunes on themselves. In strikes and look-
outs, however they originate, many are called
on to endure privations who have nothing
whatever to do with provoking or eon- ,
tinuing the quarrel. And such being the case,
it should be every humane man's duty to
limit the area over which these contentions
extend, and thus lessen the number of suf-
ferers.

Though 3,1 r. IfAura should condemn this, we
are very anxious, in the interest of employers
as well as of working mon, that such

strug,;Ples batween capital and labour should
be looked upon with disfavour by the public.

it was for this reason we condemned the
heartless and impolitic recommendation of the
editor of the Tuilders' Trades Circular. Did
this gentleman roam the forests of the new
world in his war paint, we could account for
the ferocious defiance of his whoop. Or were
he the drunken head of a faction in an Irish
fair, wild with.the excitement of personal and
party revenge, we could account for his sa-
vage advice. As matters stand, we can only
repeat that such a recommendation as a
general lock-out was simply shocking, and
such as no Englishman should be permitted to
utter without rebuke—without being told
that he had forfeited his claim to be tolerated
as an adviser where men's interests had to be
considered in a reasonable and equitable

manner.

The justification put forward by our editorial
Chocktaw fills up the measure of his iniquity,
as it proves that he quite understood the
enormity of the proposition he had the shame-
lessness to makc. Ile says that as the London
carpenters and joiners had selec Lod two firms
out of two thousand to strike against, the
other one thousand nine hundred and ninety-
eight ought to look their gates to prevent
themselves from being beaten in detail. The
logic of this is plain enough. The wisdom
and humanity of it are plain also. We have
heard this sort of thing before, but we hope
never to lack courage to rebuke it whatever
side it may come from.

If Mr. MAULT and others, whether they
seek to uphold the interests of the employers
or the employed, would try to reconcile
differences instead of widening them—to
close up breaches instead of extending them—
to advise in a spirit of peace instead of
exasperation and anger, they would be entitled
to respect and confidence. As matters stand
we can only speak of them as we feel, and we
can only regret that employers of labour for a
moment listen to such dangerous, nay such
absolutely stupid advice as they undertake to
give. It would be premature at the present
moment to volunteer any opinion as to the
way in which the present strike may termi-
nate. We hope that ere long the end will be
known, and we trust that all future differences
will find settlement by arbitration. Under
any class of circumstance such advice as that
of Mr. num; if followed, could only prolong
and embitter the struggle, and prepare the
way for repeated renewals of the fight to the
lasting injury of all concerned.

It is a common thing to complain of the
mischief done by " agitators " amongst the
men; but for intensity of virulence and medi-
tation of mischief, careless of cost or suffer-
ing, the Mlums, PIPERS, Saurus, and other
mere tools of the employers carry with them
and exercise a power to injure which working
men agitators do not possess, and which they
would not be likely to use if they did possess
it. We have no desire to find fault with
capitalists for employing such agents, but we
have a right to criticize their proceedings and
to condemn recommendations made by them,
which, if carried, would reduce such struggles
in spirit, and, in fact, to the level of those
indulged in by hungry tigers in a jungle or
starved rats in a sewer. In the interest of the
nation and for the welfare of the classes con-
cerned Lwe require a wise adjustment of the
interests now warring against each other in a
half-blind way; and these advisors of capital
at such a moment can only urge on the men
in whose service they have been enlisted, the
employment of their full energy over every
corner of the field to which the battle can be
carried. Such a spirit cannot be too strongly
condemned.

THE BIBLE IN THE SCHOOLS.
The Earl of SHIFTESBURY is "o'er-doing
Termagant" as an agitator for the Bible
in national schools. Common-place, plebian
agitators usually profess a respect for the law,
and make a parade of gaining their ends by
constitutional means. His Lordship, as a
member of the House of Peers, is above this,
and tells us plain out that if he cannot gain
his end by aid of the law, he will violate the
law to obtain them. He and those who go
with him on this question desire to make the

Bible in the schools an-instrument for the es-
tablishment of priestly power, and they
threaten to subvert public authority for the
purpose of doing so.
They desire that 'the masses of the people
should be taught to respect the powers that
be; but they will only do so themselves so
long as those powers minister to their preju-
dices, passions, and interests. Jack- CADE
has come out as a fine gentleman, with
a title and coronet, but with the oil,
determination to make his " mouth the
Parliament of England," I would " ad-
vocate rebellion," said his lordship the
other day at Birmingham, if parents wore
compelled to send their children to infidel
schools ;—meaaing by infidel schools any
schools in which the Bible teaching might not
be as his lordship would have it. The bluster
of this is perhaps all there is in it, but such
teaching addressed to the nation from the
mouth of such a man may be dangerous. lie
should remember that there are many things
to which the people attach more importance
than this about which Lord SHAFTESBURY
makes so much noise ; and it might not be
convenient if they should adopt his lordship's
rule of rebellion in reference to them. There
are fanaticisms in politics as well as in religion
and rebellion is as possible in regard to the
one as to the other. Besides, if GEORGE DIXON'
was not a more sensible man than the Earl of
SHAFTESBURY, the alternative of rebellion
might suggest itself to him on far more
dangerous grounds of probability.

' But, in truth, Lord SHAFTESBURY does not
moan rebellion when ho uses the word.
He means fanaticism the howling of
a blind bigotry. This is what he wants
• to stir up, not rebollion. He knows
how his followers can mouth and
falsify; how they can fling about ugly
epithets, such as "infidel," "godless,"
"anti-Christian," Ile knowsithere are bigots
to be aroused, ignorant fanatics to be alarmed,
interested knaveries to be j ustified. But he
should remember that the friends of honest
; unseetarian education understand the whole
trick, and know how much of braggart folly
there is in such big words, and are just as
determined as ho is, only in a solider and
quieter way; not to permit a scheme of
national education to be turned into a recruit-
ing system for dominant sects. His Lordship
of SHAFTESBURY and his friends, say what they
may, will not counsel rebellion. They are
not as fanatical as Lord GEORGE GORDON", nor
as crazy as Mr. Tilos( of Canterbury. They
are only rebellious on the platform, sounding
their gongs and beating their big drums, in
the hope of frightening their adversaries, If
they cannot get all they want, however, they
will make the best terms they can ; and
will take what they can got, though
in a dissatisfied and grumbling spirit.
They will pass, as they did at this Birmingham
meeting, very stiff resolutions as to what they
think and feel; but the nation will in spite of
this make its mind up that the public taxes
shall not be used for the teaching of sectarian
dogmas, and the consequent production of
religious strife. Besides, considering the many
generations of English children allowed to
grow up and pass away without any kind of
national instruction under the eyes of past
generation of clergymen, lords, and zealots
generally, without exciting their compassion
or care, we are not going to be deluded now
by noisy fuss about what may become of
children educated by the nation, but neglected
in religious culture by their parents. Let
Lord SHAFTESBURY and his friends look after
these and employ their zeal, their time and
their money in rectifying this defect, nobody
will quarrel with them for this. But we shall
all quarrel with them in the interest of the
nation, and fight with them to the bitter sad
rather than permit them to use the taxation
of the nation for proselytising purposes. If
these sedate and ivell-meaning persons, how-
ever, will preaoh rebellion against the law, on
this ground, we imagine that a turn or two at
the crank, with clipped hair, a suit of canary,
in one of her MAJESTY'S jailS, woufd bring the
most recalcitrant of our noble and reverend
zealots to their senses. There is no fear of
this, however; a little more platform bombast,
a blowing off of pious zeal, and, things will

10

right themselves. In tho meantime most
people will understand that the Birmingham
flourish about the Bible and rebellion is merely
one of SIIIFTESBURY'S oharaeteristies.

articles.title: QUESTION.
articles.text:
QUESTION.

The following is the continuation of the article
by Joseph Mazzini on the social ,question, now
published by the .Emancipazione

The sense of social duty towards working men
which we lately pointed out continued to increase
in men's minds (thanks especially to Republican
teaching), and to secure the popular future of re-
volutions, when there arose within the last thirty
years, particularly in France, certain schools of
men, generally good men and friends of the people,
but misled by a supreme love of system and by
individual vanity, who, under the -name of
Socialism, proposed exclusive, , exaggerated doc-
trines, often adverse to the wealth already ac-
quired by the other classes, and economically
impossible, and by alarming the multitude of
small tradesmen, and producing distrust between
various orders of Citizens, made the question retro-
gress, and divided the Republican camp. The
first effect of this distrust in France was the
more easy triumph of the Coup d'Etat. I cannot
now examine these different systems with you
one by one, which were called Saint-Simonianism,
Fourierism, Communism, and other names. Being
almost all founded Upon ideas good in themselves,
and accepted by as many as belong to the faith
of progress, they spoilt or neutralized them by the
proposed means of application which were false or.
tyrannical.. And it is necessary that I should
briefly point out to you in what they sinned,
because the promises held out to the people by
these systems are so splendid, that they might
easily mislead yOu, and you would, by embracing
them, run the risk of retarding a certain, and by
no means distant, future of emancipation. It is
true, and this should be enough to raise a power-
ful doubt in your minds, that when circumstances
call any of these men to power, they did not
attempt the practical application of their doctrine;
giants of audacity in their written pages, they
drew baele before realities.

If, while some day examining these systems atten-
tively, you remember the fundamental ideas which
I have been suggesting to you till now, and the
inseparable characteristics of human nature, you
will find that they violate all the laws of progress,
the means by which this is accomplished in
humanity, and either one or another of the
faculties which constitute man.

Progress is accomplished by laws which no
human power can break, by the gradual develop-
ment, by the perpetual modification of the elements
which manifest the activitY of life. Men have
always, at certain epochs, in certain countries, and
under the influence of certain prejudices and
• certain errors, given the name of elements, of
conditions of the social life, to things which have
no root in nature, but solely in the conventional
habits of a misguided society which, after that
epoch or beyond the limits of that country, dis-
appear. But you can discover What really are
the inseparable elements of human nature by
interrogating the instincts of your souls, and
verifying, by:the traditions of all times and of all
countries whether your instincts have always
been the instincts of humanity. And those which
an inborn voice (it is the great -voice of humanity)
points out to you as constituent elements of life,
must be modified and developed from time to time,
but. can never' be abolished.

•
Among these elements of human life, besides
religion, libert3r, association, and others indicated
in the course of this work, hi property. The prin-
ciple,
.the origin of property, exists in human
nature, and represents the needs of the individual's
material life which it is his duty to support, as,
by means of religion, of science, of liberty, the
individual is called to transform, to ameliorate, to
rule the moral and intellectual world, to transform,
to ameliorate, to rule the physical world by means
of material labour. And property is the sign, the
representation of the accomplishment of that
mission, of the amount of labour by which the
individual has transformed, developed, and in-
creased the productive forces of nature.
Property is, therefore, eternal in principle, and
you find it existent and protected throughout
the whole life of humanity. But the methods by
which property is governed are mutable, and
destined, like all other manifestations of human
life, to submit to the law of progress. Those who,
finding property constituted in a certain system,
declare that system invisible, and oppose those
who intend to change it, deny progress thereby.
It is enough to open two volumes of history
belonging to two differentperiods, to find a change
therein in the constitution of property. And those
who, finding it badly constituted at a certain
period, declare that it must be abolished, expunged
from society, deny an element of human nature,
and, could they ever succeed, would retard pro-
gress by mutilating life. Property would inevi-
tably reappear some time after, and probablY j

under the form whieh it took at the time of its
abolition.

Property is ill constituted in our day, because
the origin of the present distribution is
generally the conquest, the violence with which
in times remote from our own, certain invading
nations and classes took possession of lands and of
the fruits of labour, not their own. Property is
ill-constituted, because the basis of the distribu-
tion of the fruits of labour undertaken by the
proprietor and the operative are not founded
upon a just estimate proportionate to the libour
itself. Property is ill-constituted, beeause, con-
ferring on its possessors political and legislative
rights which are wanting to the operative; it tends
t.) being the monoply of a few and inaccessible to
the many. Property is ill-constituted, because the
system of taxation is ill-constituted, and tends to
keeping up a monopoly of wealth in the holders
of property, airgravating the situation of the
poorer classes, and taking from them all possibility
of saving. But if instead of correcting vices and
slowly modifying the constitution of property,
you vi ere to abolish it, you would suppress a
source of wealth, of emulation, and Niould resemble
the savage who, to gather the fruit, cut down the
tree.

There is no need to abolish property because it
now belongs to few; the way must be opened to
its acquisition by the many.
It tUust be brought back to the principle
which renders it leigitiinato, by so contriving that
.labour alone can produce it.
Society must be put in the way of more equal
basis of remuneration between the landowner or
capitalist and the workman.
The system of taxation must be changed, that

taxes ruay not affect the sum necessary to life,
but may leave the poor man the power of effect-
ing savings, which will, by degrees, produce pro-
perty.

And that this may happen, it is necessary to
suppress political privileges conceded to property,
and to act so that all contribute to legislative
action.

Now all these things are just and possible. By
educating yourselves to ask for thein with per-
tinacity, then to insist upon them, You will be
enabled to obtain them; while, in seeking the
abolition of property you would be seeking An
impossibility, you would be doing an injustico to
him who has obtained it by hig own labour, and
you would be diminishing instead of increasing
production.

The abolition of individual property is, never-
theless, the remedy proposed by divers of the
socialist systems of which I 4m. speaking, and
especially of Communism. Some:go beyond this;
and finding the idea of Government, the idea of
country falsified by religious errors, by privileged
men, and by the egotism of dynasties, they require
the abolition of all religion, of all Government, of all
nationality. This is acting like children or'SaVages.
Why, since foul
.air engenders disease, do they
not attempt the suppression of every breathable
gas?

I. • The ideas of those who . would in the name of
liberty found anarchy and destroy society, to leave
nettling but the individual and his rights, need no
ieflutation from nio as regards you; all my labour
opposes that guilty dream which denies progress,
duties, human brotherhood, the solidarity' of
_nations, everything which you and I venerate.
But the design of those who, 'confining thetnielves
to the economical question, ask for the abolition of
individual property end the estatliihinent of Com-
munism, tenches the other extreme, denies the
individual, denies liberty, bars the way to progress,
and, so to speak, petrifies society.
The general formula of Communism is :the
following :—The ownership of everything produc-
tive—lands, capital, moveable property, bistro-
mentli of labour—is to ,be Concentrated in the
State; the State assigns his share of labour to
each; , the State assigns to each home remunera-
finis, according to some with absolute equality,
according to. others in proportion to his needs.
This, were it ever possible, would be the lit e of
beavers, not of men.

The liberty, the dignity-, the conscience of the
individual disappear in a system of productive
machines. The physical life may be satisfied
therein; the moral life, the intellectual life aro
cancelled, and with them emulation, the free choice
of labour, free association, the stimulants to pro-
duction, the joys of prosperity, all the reasons
which induce progress. The human family is,
under this system, a flock which only needs to be
led to sufficient pasture-lands. Who among you
would resign himself to such a programme as this?
Equality is obtained, they say, which?
Equality in the distribution of labour P It is
impossible. Work is in its nature diverse, not to
be reckoned by the duration or amount of labour
performed in MI hour, but by thodiflioulty, by tlio

greater or less agreeable nature of the well:, by
the waste of vitality it produces, and by the
benefit conferred on society. How can the
equality be calculated of one hour's labour in a
mine, or in purifying the stagnant water of a
marsh, and an hour's work in a silk mill P The
impossibility of such a calculation.is such, that it has
suggested to certain among the -founders of systems
to arrange that each should in turn perform a
certain amount of work in every branch of use.
ful activity; an absurd remedy, which would
render the excellence of production impossible
unless one could succeed in suppressing the
inequalities between the weak and the robust,
between the capable and the dull, betsveen the
man of lymphatic temperament and the nittn of
nervous temperament. Work which is, easy and
pleasant to the one is difficult and heavy to the
other.

Equality in the distribution of products? It
is impossible. Either equality must bo absolute,
or it would constitute an immense injustice, not dis-
tinguishing between the different needs resultini
from organiza.tion, nor between the strength and
capacity received from nature without any merit
whatever, or equality would be relative and cal-
culated on differing needs not taking indi-
vidual production into account, would violate the
rights of property, which the workman should
have in the fruit of his labour.

Then, who would be the umpire to decide on
the needs of each individual? The State ?
Workmen, my brothers, are you disposed to
accept a hierarchy of masters of the common pro-
perty, masters of the mind by reason Of an exclu-
sive education, masters of tho body by mans of
the power of decision upon labour, upon capacity,
upon needs? Is not this a renewal of the old
slavery ? Would not these chiefs be led away by
the theory of the interests they would represent,
and, reduced by the immense power in their
hands, become founders of the hereditary dicta-
torship of the ancient caste? _

No; Communism does not establish equality
among working men ; it does not increase pro-
duction, which is the great necessity of the present
time, becautie, life being made secure, human
nature as it shows itself in most, is satisfied, and
the incentive to an•, increase of production to be
dispersed throughout all the members of the
society becomes so small that it is not sufficient to
stimulate faculty; it does not ameliorate products;
it does not encourage to progress in invention,
which will never be assisted by the uncertain
collective guidance of a system. Communism has
but one remedy to protect the sons of the people
from hunger among the evils which oppress them.
Now, cannot it do this? cannot it secure to itself
the life and labour of the workmen, without over-
throwing the whole social order, without rendering
production barren, without Cancelling the liberty
of the individual, and holding him in the chains
of a soldier-like, tyrannical system?
