articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

A deputation has waited upon the Lord
Mayor, and urged the Corporation to increase
the usefulness of Columbia Market, by eon-
struetino•'' a tramway between that institution
and the Great Eastern Railway. Memorials
in support of this request were read from the
local authorities or King's Lynn, Yarmouth,
Lowestoft, and Harwich. These were referred
to the Markets' Improvement Committee.

Mayor Hall, in his annual message, states
that the debt of the city of New York, deduct-
ing the sinking fund and the taxes due
but not yet collected amounts to 86,250,000
dols,

The eldest daughter of the unfortunate old
lady who was murdered in the Hyde-road,
Hoxton, on Wednesday last, has committed
suicide.

At the Chelmsford asAizes, on Monday,
Ellen Kettel, a married* woman 21 years of
age, was indicted for the wilful murder of
Elizabeth Kettel, her husband's first wife.
Kettel was a labourer in the service of a far-
mer at Great Bromley, and the prisoner was
his employer's daughter. The case for the
prosecution is that the accused having con-
ceived an unlawful passion for Kettel, resolved
to gratify it by poisoning his wife. The first
Mrs. Kettel died .on October 10th, 1871, and
the prisoner became Ketters second wife in
December of the same year. The trial, which
lasted the whole of the day, was adjourned.

All the members of the Geneva Tribunal
were present when it reassembled at two in
the afternoon, on Monday, after an adjourn-
ment of eighteen days, the English party
having arrived by the Paris express in the
forenoon. The sitting lasted nearly two hours,
and is understood to have been confined en-
tirely to formal arrangements for the future
procedure of the Court, ' after which the
Arbitrators adjourned. It is said that pro-
bably the Tribunal will meet every day for
the despateh of business.

B)me time ago a girl fifteen years of age,
named Catherine Alice Kinnear, prosecuted to
conviction three young men for a criminal
assault, and each of them was sentenced by
Mr. Justice Quctin to twenty years' penal
servitude. A charge of perjury was after-
wards preferred against Kinnear, and several
protracted examinations at the Guildhall
Poliee-court ended in her being committed for
trial without bail.

A correspondent, in his account of the
Gambetta banquet at Fertd-sous-Jouarre,
says that the persons present represented all
classes of sbeiety. There wore many workmen
from the town itself, several Couneillors
General of the department, and a large
number of peasants of the neighbourhood in
their blue blouses. The prioe of the tickets
was about three shillings,_ and the eorresPon-
dent points out that the French peasant does
not spend a sum like that unless he is very
much in earnest indeed. The department,
moreover, was one which suffered terribly
during the war, and. had to support many
requisitions from the German troops. M.
Gambetta was listened to with great attention,
and frequently elicited enthusiastic applause.
The utmost good order prevailed throughout
the proceedings, the only interruptions being
caused by the rain, which descended in torrents
the whole time.

A Paris Correspondent says that the anni-
versary of the taking of the Bastile was very
generally observed in many parts of the city.
Shops were shut up at an early hour, and
people in some cases went out to dine on the
Marne, beyond the limits of the state of siege,
where they were at liberty to make political
speeches and propose toasts. In Paris itself
no disorders ot any kind took place, but as a
measure of precaution strong patrols were sent
to the" fighting faubourgs.

In the French Assembly on Monday the
report of the Committee on the Loan Bill
was presented by M. Vitet, and the measure
was voted without discussion.

During the trial of a civil cause at Win-
chester the other day, Mr. Lopes, QC., M.P.,
Was cross-examining a witness, when his lord-
ship decided that a question must not be put.
Mr. Lopes repeated the question, when Mr.
Justice Mellor, with some warmth, told the
witness not to answer it. Mr. Lopes said he
wished to put before his lordship the view he
took. If counsel were not to be heard and to
state their objections, 110 distinctly said—
Mr. Justice Mellor I desire you to cease your
argument on that point. Mr. Lopes: Then I
must cease altogether if I am to be dealt with
in this way. Mr. Justice Mellor: Nothing
would give me greater pain than to fine you,
but I will if you persist in it. Mr. Lopes:
Very well, my lord. I persist in nothing.
The cross-examination was not further pro-
ceeded with.

Fifteen hundred natives of Alsace and
Lorraine marched in procession on Monday to
the French Consulate in New York and regis -
tered themselves as French citizens.

One hundred and fifteen Belgian artisans,
comprising the choir connected with the Royal
Society of the United Artisans of Belgium,
are now in London, and appeared in public
for the first time on Monday night at a concert
given at the Albert 11111. Previously to this
they had been to the Exhibition and had paid
a visit to Marlborough House.

Two men who had, after breaking into a
house in Russell-square, packed up a large
quantity of valuables, and actually put on
the coats of the people who lived in the house,
were suddenly disturbed by Mr. Charles
Lovejoy, a young man, forced to leave their
booty, and eventually captured by the police.
They have been remanded.

The German merchants and the Consul of
Hayti have protested against the recent seizure
of the corvettes by Germany, and the Consul
has resigned.

By Vice-Chancellor Malino a severe judg-
ment against possibly over-jealous trustees
has just been delivered. A young woman,
having a share in £7,000 left in 1846 by
Philip Elliot, of Neath, in Glamorgan, in
trust for his brother, and his brother's
children after his death, had been refused pay-
ment by the trustees, on grounds bitterly
denounced at the bar. She had gone to
Australia, and on her return, eight years am,
had entered an Anglican Sisterhood; cir-
cumstance on which wore founded several of
the trustees' objections to paying over the
money. Judgment was given against the
trustees, whether or not the young lady had
assigned her property to her Sisterhood; and,
as they had acted without justification, they
were called upon to indemnify the petitioner
to the last farthing of expenses.

In the Freneh Assembly on Saturday an
attempt was made by M. Magna to re-intro-
duce the proposed tax on business transactions
which had been rejected on Thursday. M.
Thiers protested against this course, and once
more affirmed that two hundred millions of
additional revenue would be required, M.
Magno having maintained that only ono
hundred and thirty-five millions were wanted.
Ultimately the House sanctioned the addition
of sixty centimes to the tax on licences, but
rejected the proposed increase of the door and
window tax and the furniture tax.

Some arrests are reported at Prague, caused,
it is said, by a plot against the life of the
governor.

The Tichborne Claimant arrived in Sunder
land on Monday, and had an enthusiastic
reception from the large crowds at the railway
station and en route to the local committee
room, where he was presented with an address.
The Claimant and M. Guildford Onslow
M.P., appeared at the balcony and harangued
the crowd; and in the evening a public meet-
ing was held in the Victoria-hall, when they
addressed the assembly.

Two tradesmen and twO costermongers were
on Saturday fined in small penalties by the
Southwark magistrate, for an offence which is
generally known as the Sunday obstruction in
the New-cut.

At Bow-street, on Saturday, Mr. Edwin
Merritt Williams was fined £lOO for keeping
a house "for the purpose of receiving money
as a consideration upon certain events and
contingencies in relation to horse-racing."
The specific charge was in oonnection with
the " Carshalton Ciroular Spec."

Additional accounts have come to hand,
showing the destructive effects of the succes-
sion of thunder storms which passed over the
northern and midland counties at the end of
last week. The tempest appears to have
visited Yorkshire and Lancashire with exeep-
tional severity.

Mr. Justice Keogh arrived at Enniskillen
on Saturday, and opened the commission for
the county Fermanagh. In reply to a strong
and unanimous address of sympathy and con-
fidence which has been voted by the grand
Jury, his lordship claimed no merit for having
done simply his duty. His attitude would be
one of patient endurance, and. he would never
be influenced by any attempt at intimidation.
The grand jury of Meath have passed a reso-
lution protesting against the continued attacks
on Justice Keogh.

His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales
has fixed the 2oth inst. as the day on which
his Royal Highness will hold a review of
school drill organized by the Society of Arts.

It is stated that 'Mr. Chaffers has instituted
an aotion for libel against Mr. Benson, the
magistrate of the Southwark Police-court, for
the expressions employed by him in his come
mots on the termination of the Twisa ease.

,At the Derby Assizes, Henry Shepherd, a
sorter in the Travelling Post-office, brought
an notion against the Midland Railway Com-
pany for damages for personal injuries re-
ceived in a railway collision between the
Newcastle train and a luggage train, at Cud-
worth, on the 15th February. He obtained a
verdiot for £Boo.—Au action brought by Mr.
John Taylor, artistic decorator, residing at
Edgware-road, London, against the Great
Western Railway Company for compensation
for injuries sustained while travelling on
their line on the 12th August last, was tried
on Monday at the Oxford Assizes. The jury
gave a verdiot for the plaintiff—damages,
£l,BOO.

Lord Shaftesbury, in presiding at the annual
meeting of the Metropolitan and Provincia
Poor Law Officers' Association, expressed his
strong conviction that unless the homes of the
people were improved, the country must some
day be overtaken with a moral pestilence,
which would overwhelm society, and bid
defiance to all their efforts.

The Criokat Match between the Eton and
Harrow public schools has been won by the
representatives of the former, with six wickets
to go down.

The annual summer fete of the Home for
Little Boys was held at the institution near
Farningham, Kent, on Saturday, when the
Prince Imperial of France was present at the
distribution of prizes, and at the laying of the
foundation-stone of a new school.

The Church of St. Mary Magdalene, Pad-
dingtbn, of which the Rev. R. Temple West
was the incumbent, was destroyed by fire on
Saturday. It was erected at a cost of over
£30,000.

An affray, which has a somewhat serious
aspect, is reported from Alexandria, in Egypt.
Shots have been exchanged between some
American officers in the Khedive's service and
the American Consul-General and his se-
cretary. One of the officers is wounded.

It is announced in a Lisbon telegram that
the unfriendly relations between Brazil and
the Argentine Republic are due to difficulties
in connection with the fulfilment of the Treaty
of Peace with Paraguay. The Brazilian
Government had determined not to receive
the Argentine Minister, and was expecting
munitions of war from Europe.

On Monday night the subject of the water
supply was discussed at the Bermondsey
Vestry, the dismission arising out of the
report of Major Bolton, water examiner to the
Board of Trade, appointed to inquire into the
grounds of the recent complaints;_ and, on
the motion of Mr. Sharpe, seconded by Mr.
APltae, a resolution was passed expressing the
opinion of the vestry that the supply of water
was totally inadequate to the requirements of
the district, and directing a copy of the same
to be sent to the Board of Trade, accompanied
by the tariff of the insurance offices, who
i have largely increased their charge of nsur-
ance on certain factories by reason of the
alleged inadequate supply.

At Wednesbury Joseph Thomas, a youth,
threw a brick at Henry. both, a boy, who was
bathing, fracturing his skull, and killing
him. Deceased had thrown a stone at
Thomas's brother.

An appeal has been addressed to the work-
ing men and women of the Bast-end, urging
them to agitate for the opening of the Bethnal.
green Museum on tho Sunday. Persons
favourable to the movement are requested to
communicate by letter with Mr. J. T. Giles,
H, South-place, Finsbury.

It has transpired that on the arrival at Mel-
bourne of the last two mails from England, a
large quantity of jewellery was seized at the
Post-office by the Customs authorities. The
importers of the jewellery, instead of passing
entries for it at the Customs and paying the
usual duty, have, by an arrangement with
the English exporter, been in the habit of
getting it sentout enclosed in registered paokets.
One firm received in this manlier no less than
87 valuable rings, and the difference between
the amount expended for postage and that
payable as duty was something enormous.

The ships comprising the American squadron
will assemble in the Southampton Waters in
a few days, when a public banquet is proposed
to be given to Admiral Alden and the officers.
It is understood that on the 31st instant the
Prince and Princess of Wales will visit the
fleet.

Tin Juno return of the number of diseased
foreign animals brought by sea to ports in
Groat Britain, just published by the Privy
Council Ofllee, gives a t )t,1,1 of 622 head. Of
these 306 were cattle, 256 she .p, and 100
swine. Forty of the sheep were allected with
seab, and were re-shipped to Norway; the
rest were slaughtered at the places of
lauding.

It is expected that the Minotaur and the
Bellerophon will return to Portsmouth in
about a fortnight, and that a court-martial
will then be held there to inquire into the
reoent collision between the two vessels.

The Yew York Tribune writes as follows of
the intense heat in New. York :—Seventy
persons dropped dead from the heat in a single
day, and the hospitals are crowded with
delirious victims. The night brings no rest,
for it is as hot as the day. From the tene-
ment quarters crowds of half-dressed men and
women and children hurry, when darkness
comes on, to the parks and open squares, and
the steps and porticoes of public buildings.
In houses of the better class people toss all
night sleepless on their heated beds, or pass
the midnight boars at the windows longing
for the cool breeze which never comes, and
fretting over the oppression which is never
relaxed. The wretchedness is universal; and
to hundreds, whose occupations expose them
especially to the influence of the sun, such a
heat brings not merely suffering but death.

At the Warwick Assizes the other day, a
young lady, the daughter of a farmer, ob-
tained .£250 damages for broach of premise Of
marriage. The defendant, a farmer, was
shown to have purchased. recently a farm
which cost X5OO. The defence was that there
never was any promise, and that the whole
story of the plaintiff was a fabrication.

At courts-martial on board the Duke o-
Wellington at Portsmouth on Monday,
Caps
tam a the Hon. H. C. Glyn prosiding—Thoma-
John Chapman, a seaman on board the Serat
pis, was sentenced to two years' imprisonment "
in Lewes gaol for deserting from the ship on
the 29th of June; James Symonds, a marine
on board the Resistance, was sentenced to
seven months' imprisonment, with hard la-
bour, for disobeying the lawful orders of two
sergeants, and using abusive language to
them; and Henry Smith and William Brown,
seamen belonging to the Duke of Wellington,
were sentenced to two years' imprisonment,
and dismissal from the service, for deserting
from the ship, and taking a gig away with
them.

Rear-Adtniral Prevost-Fairfax, who has
been staying in Berlin in connection with the
San Juan Boundary Question, has left for
Stettin.

lir. Gibbs, the head of the well-known firm
of Antony 'Gibbs and Son, it is said, has given
£30,009 to Keble College, Oxford, for the
purpose of building a chapel for the youngest
of the Oxford colleges.

There was a numerous attendance at the
final sitting of the International Prison Con-
gress; Sir John Pakington presiding. The
report of the General Committee, in present-
ing a resume of the proceedings, expressed
an opinion that in the general ques-
tion of reclamation, the influence of women
devoted to such work was of the. highest
importance, and the Committee rejoiced that
the Congress' had had the 'advantage of the
presence and counsel of many ladies whose
practical acquaintance with prieons and re•
formatories had given.. weight to. their words,
and whose example furnished hope for the
future.

On Saturday night a farmer named Ryan,
and his son, about twenty years old, residing
at Inchaquill, county Tipperary, were attacked
about a mile outside the town of Tipperary, by
seven men, who suddenly started from behind
a ditch. The father, after receiving some
blows, ran in the direction of Tipperary, while
the son escaped towards Coppainore police
barrack; but a travelling showman whom
they had casually met on the road, being
taken for one of themselves, was knocked
down, and so severely injured .that hi s life is
despaired of. Three men named Allen, Trahy,
and Ryan have been arrested, and identified
by young Ryan. The outrage is conjectured
to be agrarian, as Ryan bad recently purchased
for X 1,500 a farm, for which some others also
bid. He and his son bad been in Tipperary
town to lodge part of the purl:phase money in
the bank, and were returning home when they
were attacked.

The Bishop of Gloucester and Bristol has
come upon an early MS. of the Athanasian
Creed in the public library at Utreeht—a very
early copy he believes, as early as the seventh
century at least, which contains the damnatory
clauses in their perfection. Canon Swainson
does not think it is so old, but if the opinion
of the paheographer who assigns it to the
seventh century is confirmed, as we believe it
will be, we suppose nobody will have the
courage to object to clauses which go back as
far as the seventh century.—Speetator.

There is a great dist atisfaction at Woolwich
respeJting the fretineut absence of the Royal
Artillery hand. 'The htter is so frequently
employe'l in fulfilling engagements at a die-
tatiae that the officers of the corps derive very
little benefit from their own musicians.

JULY 2O, 1872.

The Swiss Times says that at the condensed
milk manufactory in Chain there are said to be
10,000 quarts of thilk condensed every day,
and as many more in the branch establishments
at Gossau (Canton St. Gall) and Dudingen
(Canton Friburg) taken together. Four-fifths
of this condensed. milk goes to London. The
milk so timployed, reckoning the quart at 20
centimes, costs daily 4,000 francs ; other
materials, such as the sugar and the tin cases,
come to at least 6,000 francs, which together
makes a daily outlay of 10,000 francs (1300)
for raw material alone.

The jury engaged in New York, in the trial
of. Stokes, the assassin of Mr. J. Fisk, jun:,
have been unable to agree on a vordict, and
have been dismissed.

Noisy manifestations have been made during
the last few days against the Jesuit establiEh-
meat in Brest, in consequence of scandalous
reports affecting a Jesuit priest. On Sunday
evening the gendarmerie were compelled to
disperse an assemblage and make a few arrests.
A proclamation of the mayor recommends
tranquillity, and says that a judicial inquiry
will be commenced respecting the reports in
question.

A Times telegram, from Berlin, says that
the Russian Press is again placed under the
supervision of the administrative authorities.

A. marriage has been arranged between
Lady A.lice WOdehouse, eldest daughter of the
Earl and Countess of. Kimberley, and Mr.
Hussey Paeke, only son of Lieutenant-Colonel
Puke, late. M.P. for South Lincolnshire.

The Free Church Presbytery of Dnndee had
again under consideration on Monday the
charge against the Rev. Mr. Knight, of having
preached in the chapel of the .Rev.. James
Martineau, London. Mr. Knight made a
tatethent adhering to his former position.
After a long disoussion, the Presbytery with
one disentient, resolved to censure Mr. Knight,
and to require him to repudiate the Unitarian
body as forming any part of the Church of
Christ. A deputation present from Mr.
Knight's congregation declared that they:
identified themselves with their minister.

It is now said that her Majesty will Lot pay
a flying visit to St. Andrew's during her brief
titay at Elolyrood next month.

It is said that Oaptain Keogh, brother of
the
,judge, attended a country Roman'Catholic
obapel near Enniskillen on Sunday. Judge
Keogh was denounced from the altar, upon
which •Captain Keogh left the chapel and was
followed by, a number of the congregation,
who displayed an attitude so threatening that
ho was obliged to be protected by police. An
attempt was made on Saturday night to burn
the effigy of Justice Keogh, On Monday the
effigy burners were committed for trial.

The Belgian journals mention that M. Van
Bastelaere, recently appointed Burgomaster at
Waohtebeke, was •attacked in the streets a
few nights back by several individuals with
blackened faces, and was injured so seriously
that he has since died. Politicnl animosity is
believed to be the motive of this outrage. '

The Czar is to proceed to Moscow as soon as
the mananwres of the Russian army are
terminated. Afterwards, he will proceed to
the Crimea, to remain until the end of Sep-
tember. Consequently, his Majesty cannst be
present at the interviews of the Emperors of
Germany and Austria, as the Berlin journals
lately announced.

Lord. Chief. Justice Whiteside,, in ope,ning,
the. Meath Assizes, on Monday, said a most'
satisfactory change had occurred sines he last
addressed'them, and 'there were on this °cm;
sion only three cases-for trial. The Crown
Soliaitor- had also made a report comparing
the present state
,of the eouuty with 'its
condition two years ago. - That report was
also most, aati.sfactory, .end the change had
been ascribed by Mr. Seeds to the recent
Acts of Parliament for the better proteotion of
life and property.

Adviees from Belgrade states that the
Sultan has amnestied nil the chiefs and.
partisans of the last Bosniae revolution.
Fezlih Puha, the general of the insurgents,
has even been promoted to a high post at
Travnik.

It has been decided in Legitimist circles
to send to the Comte de Chambord an ad-
dress of loyalty, to be presented by throe
delegates (aou-deputies) on St. Henry's day.

Tho oonstruotion of a tramway from Pim-
lico, via Vauxhall-bridge, to Kennington and
Camberwell is now completed, and the line
will be opened for public traffic in a few weeks.
The toll derived from the cars running over
the bridge will amount to £l,OOO a-year, A
complete and direct route from Greenwich to
Pimlico and the West End will thus be opened
out.

Replying to an address from the Tyrone
Grand jury on .Tuesday, Mr. Justice Keogh
stated that he should not stoop to explain or
justify anything he had said or done, nor
would he surrender his trust to the dictates or
menaces, secret or open' of any person, body
or power.. "Without distinction of person,
profession, or class, I shall continue faithfully
and fearlessly to administer and expound the
law of England, and no other."

At Baron Van de Weyer's residence the
Belgian Choral Society of Workmen sang the
"Tyrol," by A. Thomas; "La Retraite, ' by
Soubre (solos by MM. De Ville and Bouque) ;
"Le Cho3ur des Jannissaires," by Limnander
(the solo by M. De Ligne), under the direction
of Mr. Lintermans ; and "Le Chant d'Araour
par Otto," under, the direction of Mr. De Mol.
They afterwards went to Westminster Abbey,
where they had the honour of singing before
Dean and Lady Augusta Stanley and other
ladies and gentlemen in the green plot behind
the Abbey, and the cloisters. The Dean after-
wards kindly invited them to partake of re-
freshments in his own house. in the evening
the managers of the Alhambra kindly gave
them free admission.

A meeting of labourers employed at Chat-
ham Dockyard has been held, for the purpose
of considering the best means to adopt to ob-
tain an increase of wages. The movement
was in connection with similar ones at the
other Gdvernment yards, and it was shown
how utterly impossible it was for the labourers
who were receiving 14s. a week to maintain a
wife and four or five children, or provide for
them the common necessaries of life. The
meeting unanimously resolved to memorialize
the Admiralty, and continuo the agitation
until an increase of pay be obtained. Than k
were given to Mr. Otway, M.P., Mr. Martin,
M.P., and all members of Parliament who
have advocated the cause of the labourers.

On Tuesday evening a party of three boys
while bathing and fishing in a river at Taun-
ton met their deaths by drowning. The bodies
were at once recovered, Their ages were
between seven and eleven. Several persons
were on'the spot, but were powerless to save
the lads.

The following is said to be the text of the
letter from Queen Victoria to the King of
Burinah which has been delivered to the latter
with much pomp and ceremony :—" Balmoral
Palace, Sept. 23, 1871.—T0 his Majesty the
King of Burmah.—My friend,—l have received
with heartfelt gratification your Majesty's most
acceptable letter. I have heard from time to
time with much pleasure of your Majesty's
friendly inclinations, and of the enlightened
i manner n which you have encouraged coin-
menial intercourse between your own and the
British Provinces, and otherwise, by your own
amicable dispositions and your wise policy,
have contributed to the maintenance of peace,
and the extension of civilization. By Allah
interchanges of good feeling between sovereign
States, the prosperity of empire, and the hap-
piness of nations are much promoted, and it
will always be a satisfaction to me to receive
tidings of the continued welfare of your
Majesty and of the people who are subject to
your rule. Iroping that you may long be
spared to govern the country committed to
your care by the Almighty Disposer of events,
—I am, your Majesty's sincere friend) Vic-
TORIA, R.

From Turkey two items of news have
arrived. The Order of the Medjidie has been
conferred upon Mehomed Tirkik Paella, son
and heir presumptive to the Khedive of Egypt;
and Mgr. Hassoun, the Armenian Patriarch,
who, having been appointed by the Pope, has
been deposed by the Porte, is preparing to
leave the country.

The Essex poisoning case, in which a far-
mer's daughter, who, it is alleged, fell madly
in love with one of her father's labourers, and
poisoned his wife in order to marry him, is
charged as a murderess, came to an abrupt
termination on Tuesday morning, the prisoner
having been delivered during the night of a
male child. The jury were consequently
discharged, and the ease adjourned till the
23rd, October.

Under pretence of selling a newspaper,
Patrick Molloy, an ill-conditioned lad ot 18
years, picked the pocket of a customer of a
gold watch. A bystander, however, captured
him as he was making off, and Alderman Sir
Sydney Waterlow, sitting at the Mansion
House, sent him for trial.

The introduction of Polo, or hookey on
horseback, into the list of English sports,
was marked by the presence of the Prince and
Princess of Wales, the Duke and Duchess of
'lo3k, and a fashionable company, who assem-
bled in the Great Park at Windsor, to witness
a contest between six officers of the Blues and
six of the Oh Lancers. The game, which
lasted for two hours, and gave considerable
delight to the spectators, furnishing as it did
examples of splendid horsemanship, resulted
in a draw,

The competition which is of the greatest
interest at Wimbledon—that for the Queen's
Prize—was brought to a close on Tuesday,
when Colour-Sergeant W. Michie, of the Lon-
don Scottish, wai declared the winner. iTe had
made 63 points, while last year the successful
number was 68, and the fortunate volunteer
was Lieutenant Humphry, of the Cambridge
University Corps. Sergeant Michie was car-
ried in triumph to the Council tent, and after-
wards to the regimental camp of the London
Scottish. The prizes will be presented on
Saturday by the Princess of Wales.

The annual meeting of the Society for the
Protection of Life from Fire was held at the
Guildhall on Tuesday, the Lord Mayor in the
chair,

A telegram from Alexandria states that a
Military Commission is sitting there to inquire
into the circumstances connected with the
serious affray between Americans which re-
eently took place. Colonel Butler, the
American Consul-General, who is onncerned
in the matter, has meanwhile left for Europe.

As a result of the Royal Warrant regulating
the promotion in the Scientific Corps of the
Army, a large number of first captains in the
Engineers and Royal Artillery were on
Tuesday night gazetted as majors.

According to the weekly report of the Regis-
trar-General, the mean temperature last week
was 631 deg., and 1.2 deg. above the average
for the same week in 50 years; the menu
temperature of the water of the Thames was
67.2 deg. Not quite three-quartets of an inch
of rain fell at the Royal Observatory, Green-
wich, while the amount exceeded three
inches in Hull, Leeds, Nottingham, Liver-
pool, and Sheffield, and in Salford the remark-
able quantity of 5.80 inches was measured.

At Guildhall, a youth named Hedger was
sent to prison for one month with hard
labour for having assaulted his mother. At
the Lambeth court, Jonathan Kemble, 28
years of age, was sentenced to four months of
the like punishment for an offence similar in
character, but more exaggerated in degree.

Last week the aggregate mortality in
London and 20 other large towns in the
United Kingdom was at the rate of 20 deaths
annually to every 1,000 persons estimated to be
Jiving. In the metropolis 2,172 births and
1,285 deaths were registered, the former
having been 7, and the latter 191 below the
average. Twenty-sir persons died from
measles, 12 from scarlet fever, 3 from diph-
theria, 68 from whooping-cough, 20 from
different forms of fever (of ' which 4 were
certified 'as typhus, 11 as enteric or tyithoid,
and 5 as simple continued fever), and 148
from diarrho3a. The usual summer epidemic
of diarrlicoa Appears to have set in. The
deaths referred to this disease in London,
which in the two previous weeks had been 37
and 61 rose last week to 148, of which 121
were of infants under one year of age, and 16
of children between one and five years,

At the Portland Convict establishment a day
or two since, one of the prisoners complained
of illness, but Dr. APLean, summoned to at-
tend upon him, refused to prescribe, the man
showing no symptoms of sickness. On the
doctor descending the staircase the convict
threw a small form upon him. Re now lies
in a precarious condition, suffering from the
effects of the blow. The warders immediately
scoured the convict and lodged him in a cell.

Prince Bismarck is expected to spend a few
months at Torquay.

The death was announced on Wednesday of
Lady Byles, the wife of the Hon. Sir J. B.
Byles, one of the Judges of the Court of Com-
mon Pleas.

The Mayor of Weymouth has received a
letter, intimating that it is very probable their
Royal Highnesses the Prince and Princess of
Wales will honour Weymouth with a visit
early next month, for the purpose of declaring
the breakwater open. His Royal Highness is
expected to visit Portland in his yacht.

• The Chancellor of Cambridge University
has received a communication, stating that it
is the intention of Lord Portsmouth to
_pre-
sent to the University all Sir Isaac New-
ton's manuscripts, •with the exception of
those relating to private affairs, and that his
lordship wiskes the transfer should be pro-
ceeded with at as early a period as possible.

Prince Arthur has accepted the invitation
of the Earl of liarewood to stay at ihrewood
House on the occasion of his Royal High.
ness's visit to Leeds to open Roundhay-park
on Thursday, the 19th September.

An order issued at Aldershot on Monday
for a flying column to march to Wimbledon
on Tuesday smorning was countermanded in
the afternoon, a telegram having been re-
ceived from the Horse Guards that the column
was not to proceed to Wimbledon.

articles.title: LATEST INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.
The Guards' Band has returned from Boston
Jubilee.
An afternoon entertainment will bo given
to-day at the Mansion House to raise funds
to build an infant nursery and mission room
for the children seamen and others in con-
nection with St. Paul's, Dock-street, London
Docks.

As anticapted, theldirectors of the Bank of
England have just announced an advance
from 3 to 31 per cent, in the rate of dis-
count.

The British siction of the International
Working Men's Association will hold its first
annual Congress at Nottingham on Sunday and
Monday next.
The Marseilles journals speak of a very
destructive conflagration in tho oil manu-
factory of MM. Tschiffeli Brothers, line
Fontaine-Saint-Lazare, in that city. The
loss, which was very considerable, is only
made up to the extent of 400,000 francs by

A meeting of the Internationale is convened
for the 2nd of September, at the Hague, for
revising the statutes, so as to cope with the
late legislative measure.
The dockyard labourers at Chathank,have
held another meeting to endeavour to obtain
an increase of their wages from the Admiralty.,
The unskilled labourers at present receive 14s.
a week, and the men urge that at any time
the pay is too low, while now the increased
and inoreasing pace of
.the necessaries of life
make the wages quite inadequate for the

Extensive preparations are being made at
Woolwich for the approaching Autumn
Manceuvres. Waggons and stores of various

use of the different regiments, and detach-
ments of men belonging to the Guards and a
number of Infantry regiments are undergoing
a course of training under the Army Service
Corps to enable them to act as regimental
transports. .

Telegraph Company, has sent the following
despatch from the company's manager in
Egypt :—" Mr. Henry Stanley, from Zanzibar,
left Port Said yesterday for England, via
Marseilles, per French steamer, in company
with Dr. Livingstone's son."
The managing director of the Staveley
Colliery has given the colliers an advance of
6 per cent. on their wages, and pro-
mised them more after a while. The price of
coal on the pit bank is now double what it was
a year ago.

The Grand Jury of _Kerry have passed a
resolution to the effect that a memorial should
be presented to the Chief Secretary of Ireland,
calling upon him to recommend the Govern-
ment to step in and take charge of the Irish
railways.

Eleven more of the dead bodies washed from
the Manchester cemetery, by the recent flood
were recovered yesterday—ten in the River
bledlock and one in the Bridgewater Canal.

to seventy.

quired to quell a disturbance in the Seven
Dials on the previous night. Several of the
officers were injured—one of them so severely

ASSISTANTS.

Another meeting of the Metropolitan Shop.
keepers' Assistants' Association was held, on
Sunday evening, under the presidency of Mr. G.
Linnams Banks. Miss Amelia Lewis addressed the
meeting, and urged the necessity of a cessation
• from labour on Sundays in Order to obtain proper
recreation and rest from the exertions of the
week. The chairman announced a donation of £5
from Sir John Lubbock, and stated that Lady
Lubbock was using her influence with the West.
end shopkeepers to induce them to close upon the
7th of August next. A choesemonger addressed
the meeting., and considered that the linendrapers
had little to complain of in working from seven
in the morning until nine at night, as it was no

was carried to the effect that, as the public had
not responded to the appoals made for support,
this
meeting pledges itself to support the associa-
tion as the most likely means of redressing the
grievances of metropolitan shop assistants.

articles.text:
LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

On Wednesday the weekly meeting of this
Board was held in the Court of Sewers
Boom, the usual place of meeting, the Council
Chamber, being in course of preparation for
• the ceremony in connection with the presen-
tation of the freedom of the City to Baroness
'Burdett Coutts. Lord Lawrence presided.
Mr. Watson, in moving that the Statistical
Committee be empowered to employ such paid
assistance as they nay think proper for ob-
taining the information required by the
Board, stated that the result of the inquiries
which had already been set on foot by the
committee was as follows": The committee had
found that there are in the metropolis 681,101
children between 3 and 13 years old; of these,
01,307 were above 9 years of age and 9,161
were in institutions. These two age,
added
together made a total of 106,408 children
whom the Board would not have to look after.
Then there remained 574,693 to be taken into
consideration. From the latter figures should
be deducted 325,688 children who were pro.
vided for in schools efficient and already pro-
vided and proposed, and a proportion of send-
efficient schools. The number of children left
was 239,105. Upwards of a quater of a million
of children thus required to be seen after. The
Board proposed to deal with 100,600 of these
children, leaving more than 150,000 to be
cared for by some other means. Add the pro-
bable increase in the population within the
next couple of years, and they, woad have
something like 135,000 children for whom
education ought to be provided. He felt
bound to mention those facts in consequence of
very erroneous statements on the subject
having been published. If the parties who
were in the habit of thus covertly attacking
the Board would, instead of so acting, endea-
vour to assist the Board in encountering the
difficulties which had to be overcome, he be-
lieved that the Board would be able to accom-
plish the whole work satisfactorily in twelve
months. (Hear, hear.) The Board would
perceive that the deductions made were 22 per
cent. instead of only 5 per cent., as had been
said. He hoped that he would hear no more
of this matter. After a short discussion the
motion of Mr. Watson was agreed to.
The Finance Committee, in a report pre-
sented on their behalf by Mr. Freeman, called
to mind that the Board had resolved to borrow
£250,000 from the Public Works Lorin Com-
missioners, and that the first loan of £lOO,OOO
had been granted.
